questions.q: What must be enabled and deployed before Salesforce can be turned on as an Identity Provider?
options: A Connected App with full access scope
Einstein Analytics
Multi-Factor Authentication for every user
My Domain
questions.explain: My Domain must already be enabled and deployed, since Salesforce needs a stable, org-specific domain to serve as the basis for the Issuer/Entity ID values in the assertions it signs as an IdP.

questions.q: What does enabling the Identity Provider feature at the org level actually do?
options: It makes Salesforce capable of acting as an IdP and generates/selects the certificate it will sign assertions with
It disables all SAML Single Sign-On Settings
It converts all users to have admin access
It immediately configures trust with every external system Salesforce will ever talk to
questions.explain: Enabling the feature is a prerequisite step — it makes Salesforce capable of being an IdP and sets up the signing certificate, but doesn't yet define which service providers it vouches for.

questions.q: What does a Service Provider definition specify?
options: The connected app's Consumer Secret rotation schedule
The user's password policy
The external application's Entity ID, ACS URL, and which Salesforce attribute maps to its expected subject
The org's session timeout
questions.explain: A Service Provider definition tells Salesforce, as the IdP, which external application to issue assertions for and how to address them (Entity ID, ACS URL, subject mapping).

questions.q: When Salesforce acts as the IdP for several downstream applications, what becomes architecturally significant about Salesforce's own identity hygiene?
options: Downstream apps no longer need their own authorization rules
Only the downstream apps' security matters, not Salesforce's
Nothing changes; downstream apps have independent security regardless
Salesforce's user deactivation process and MFA enforcement become the single point controlling access to every downstream app relying on it
questions.explain: If Salesforce is the authoritative IdP for multiple apps, failures in Salesforce's own identity hygiene (like a delayed deactivation) cascade to every system that trusts Salesforce's assertions.

questions.q: In a SAML trust relationship where Salesforce is the IdP, what does the external SP use to validate the signed assertions it receives?
options: Salesforce's signing certificate, generated or selected when the Identity Provider feature was enabled
The SP's own Consumer Secret
A shared static API key
The user's Salesforce password
questions.explain: The SP validates Salesforce's signature against the certificate Salesforce used when it was configured as an IdP — the mirror image of Salesforce validating an external IdP's certificate in Lesson 4.
